sections.title: Speech movements in MRI
teaching: Speech involves coordinated movement inside the vocal tract. The MRI sequences expose changing tongue shapes and changing openings between the lips, tongue, and roof of the mouth. Much of this movement is hidden when we watch a speaker from outside.
The tongue changes shape while the jaw and lips also move. A speech gesture therefore involves relationships among moving structures, rather than a single isolated body part.

sections.title: Why speech is a remarkable learned skill
teaching: Children learn extremely complex movements of their speech organs with very little explicit instruction and little direct visual feedback about those organs. By roughly ages 2–4, they can use a large vocabulary and much of the structure of adult language.

Recognizing alphabet shapes does not by itself produce fluent reading and writing. Reading and writing whole words develop around ages 6–7 in the course comparison and require substantial instruction. The contrast concerns how much explicit teaching these skills ordinarily receive.

Articulatory phonetics studies how the structures of the vocal tract move to produce speech. MRI makes internal tongue and vocal-tract movement visible even though a person speaking normally cannot watch most of those movements.
Voice assistants and other speech technologies emulate aspects of human speech. Understanding both the human system and the artificial system connects speech science with technology.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics
teaching: The air between the tongue and the surrounding vocal tract can vibrate. Articulatory movements change the shape of that air space, while acoustic phonetics studies the sound produced by vibration in it.

A curved vocal tract can be simplified into a straight tube when the goal is to understand the motion of its air. In the Schwa animation, rows of air particles move back and forth along the tube. Their changing spacing creates regions where air is more crowded and regions where it is less crowded.

The particles oscillate around local positions while the pattern of crowding changes along the tube. The schematic therefore connects the visible space above the tongue with the physical vibration that carries speech sound.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters
teaching: AI can have psychological, economic, social, and environmental consequences. The course also names possible benefits in immunotherapy and environmental engineering, so scientific understanding matters for evaluating both its uses and its harms.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning
teaching: Habit, memorization, specialized skills, repetition, and replication provide familiar ways of responding to familiar situations. They can encourage treating similar things as identical and small differences as decisive.

Creative reasoning also asks whether very different things share the same underlying structure, or whether superficially similar things differ in an important way. Posing questions and answering them repeatedly connects everyday knowledge with insight and problem solving.

The higher goals in Diotima’s ladder include thought, focus, attention, imagination, vision, critical reading, and creative writing. Iskarous uses the ladder to emphasize explaining and discovering relationships rather than relying entirely on repeated textbook answers.

The comparison runs from Diotima around 440 BCE to the lecturer’s account of interviews in 2026. The claim that interviews increasingly reward those higher skills is the lecturer’s educational argument.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives
teaching: Sustain f as in fat and then v as in vat. Keep the place of the narrow constriction similar while changing whether the vocal folds vibrate. The first sound is voiceless and the second is voiced.

The same contrast occurs between th in thing and th in that, between s in sing and z in zing, and between sh in mesh and the sound written j here in beige. The j label refers to the sustained sound in beige, not the initial sound of an ordinary English word such as jump.

Voicing concerns vibration of the vocal folds. Place of articulation concerns where the vocal tract narrows. Moving from f/v through the two th sounds, s/z, and sh/j changes the constriction location while preserving the possibility of a voiced–voiceless pair.

sections.title: The fricative system
teaching: Fricatives allow air through a narrow constriction. The table organizes them by place horizontally and by vocal-fold vibration vertically, so a change of row and a change of column represent different physical changes.

At the labial place, f is voiceless and v is voiced. Their constriction is at the lips and teeth. At the dental place, th in thing is voiceless and th in that is voiced, with the tongue near the teeth.

At the alveolar place, s is voiceless and z is voiced, with the constriction toward the ridge behind the upper teeth. At the postalveolar place farther back, sh is voiceless and the sound written j in beige is voiced.

The MRI sequences compare the position of the narrowing across those four places. The narrowing shifts from the front of the mouth toward the region behind the alveolar ridge. Voicing can change while the general location of the constriction stays the same.
issues: The source uses j for the voiced postalveolar fricative in beige. This is the source’s informal label.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality
teaching: Stops involve a complete closure somewhere in the oral tract. The first row groups p, b, and m at the lips. The middle row groups t, d, and n at the alveolar ridge. The bottom row groups k, g, and ng at the velum, with the back of the tongue raised.
Within the oral stops, p, t, and k are voiceless, while b, d, and g are voiced. Their place pairs are p/b, t/d, and k/g. The place stays similar within a pair while vocal-fold vibration changes.

The nasal sounds m, n, and ng are voiced and share the oral closure locations of those three place groups. Their nasal airflow distinguishes them from the oral plosives. The MRI comparisons therefore separate where a closure is made from whether voicing is present and whether air can pass through the nose.
issues: The title Stops includes both oral and nasal stops. The nasal sounds are not classified as oral plosives.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge
teaching: Consonants can be organized by manner, voicing, and place of articulation. Manner concerns how airflow is restricted. Voicing concerns whether the vocal folds vibrate. Place concerns where the restriction occurs.

For fricatives, the voiceless row contains labial f, dental th, alveolar s, and postalveolar sh. The corresponding voiced row contains v, the th of that, z, and the j sound of beige. No velar fricative is listed in this table.

For oral stops or plosives, the voiceless row contains labial p, alveolar t, and velar k. The voiced row contains b, d, and g in those same columns. The table lists no dental or postalveolar plosives.

The voiced nasal stops are labial m, alveolar n, and velar ng. A sound can therefore share its place and voicing with another sound while differing in manner, as m and b do. Knowing English speech involves this structured system even when a speaker has never consciously named its dimensions.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure
teaching: Wilson L. Taylor’s 1953 article, “Cloze Procedure” A New Tool for Measuring Readability, treats completion of missing language as a measurable behavior. It appeared in the Fall 1953 issue of Journalism Quarterly.

The article introduced the method and its theory through three pilot studies and two experiments. Cloze results were compared with two readability formulas. The research question was whether people’s ability to restore deleted parts of a message could help measure how readable or communicatively effective that message was.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern
teaching: Closure is the tendency to complete a familiar but unfinished pattern. A broken circle can be recognized as a whole circle because familiarity with its shape lets the viewer mentally close the gap. The three incomplete black disks also support an apparent shape in the empty region between them.

Cloze is pronounced like the verb close and takes its name from closure. Taylor extends the same principle from visual patterns to language. The reader uses the context that remains to reconstruct something missing.

The original research describes cloze as a psychological tool for measuring effective communication. Its data can be quantified by counting successful restorations. Its initial tests concerned readability in three pilot studies and two experiments, and its results were compared with the Flesch and Dale–Chall readability measures.

The article reports initial agreement with those measures and then a broader comparison against them. It describes possible theoretical and practical applications in communication as possibilities for further investigation, rather than already established outcomes.

Taylor acknowledges Charles E. Osgood and Melvin R. Marks for instigating and assisting the work. The printed footnote also credits Lee J. Cronbach, Wilbur Schramm, Charles E. Swanson, George R. Klare, participating journalism teachers, Kalmer E. Stordahl, and Clifford M. Christensen for advice, assistance, or contributions.

sections.title: What successful completion requires
teaching: In “Chickens cackle and ___ quack,” ducks fills the gap. A correct restoration counts as one cloze unit when it reproduces the word that was deleted. A cloze unit therefore records a successful recovery from the context that remains.

Completion requires more than knowing one isolated word. The reader uses word meanings, familiar word forms, relationships between words, and the parallel sentence structure linking chickens with cackle and ducks with quack. The whole pattern constrains what belongs in its missing part.

A cloze procedure begins with a message from a writer or speaker, deletes selected parts, and presents the incomplete message to readers or listeners. Their attempts to restore its parts provide a set of measurable cloze units.

Knowledge can be tested through the ability to complete a sequence. For the language-model account used in this course, predicting an appropriate completion is the operational way knowledge becomes visible in the output.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge
teaching: The input word vectors are called x’s. Numbers called weights, or w’s, determine how the system transforms those inputs into a probability distribution over possible next words.

The computation combines inputs with weights using operations built from addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Elementary operations can produce a complex transformation when used in a very large interconnected system.

The learned knowledge resides in the weights that shape this transformation. The course describes some large AI systems as having trillions of weights. Changing the weights changes which completions receive high or low probability for the same input.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning
teaching: Learning from an error requires a way to compare a current response with relevant observations. The discrepancy identifies how the current estimate should change.

Stochastic gradient descent uses repeated observations to improve an estimate. Averaging is a simple case in which the effect of correction can be followed directly. The motivational comparison between theory, practice, and mistakes emphasizes the value of feedback, rather than presenting measured quantities of learning.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning
teaching: For the three numbers 10, 12, and 14, adding the values and dividing by three gives 12. That direct arithmetic method produces their average when all three values are available.

Complex examples such as speech, language, biological molecules, and scenes do not reduce to adding a few observed numbers. The course therefore uses a different way of learning the average as a model for a more general learning process.

Begin with a guess x, compare it with one observed value from the list, and move the guess part of the way toward that observation. Repeat with another value. Each correction changes the estimate because new evidence exposes a discrepancy. This is observation-based error learning.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent
teaching: The data are [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72]. Begin with the arbitrary estimate x[0] = 130, then randomly observe d[0] = 98. The signed discrepancy is 130 − 98 = 32, so this observation is lower than the current estimate.

The learning rate controls how much of that discrepancy is corrected. With a rate of 10%, the update is x[1] = 130 − 3.2 = 126.8. The estimate falls toward 98 without being replaced by that single observation.

Repeatedly select an observation, compare it with the current estimate, and correct a fraction of the difference. Stochastic refers to the random observation. Gradient identifies a loss-related direction for change. Descent concerns reducing error rather than a requirement that the numerical estimate always decrease.
issues: This slide calls the signed discrepancy Loss. Later lecture examples explicitly distinguish signed discrepancy from nonnegative squared loss.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability
teaching: Each panel plots the estimate x on the vertical axis against epochs from 0 to 300 on the horizontal axis. Red begins at 130, green at 80, and blue at 10. The three initial conditions approach the same general region near the data average of about 80.

At a 10% learning rate, the high red estimate drops and the low blue estimate rises fairly quickly. Once they reach the central region, all three estimates continue to fluctuate modestly because each sampled observation can pull them in a different direction.

At 50%, the initial correction is much faster, but the estimates fluctuate more strongly around the central region. At 80%, the estimates make still larger changes in response to individual observations and remain especially variable.

At 1%, red decreases and blue increases much more slowly. Even by epoch 300, the blue estimate remains below the central region and red approaches it from above. The green estimate stays close to 80 with small fluctuations because it begins near the average and uses small corrections.

A large learning rate gives each observation more influence. That makes the initial response faster but also makes an estimate near the average more vulnerable to being pulled away by a particular data point. A small rate reduces that jitter but requires more observations to travel far from a poor initial guess.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff
teaching: Increasing the learning rate γ increases how quickly an estimate reacts to observations. It also increases the continuing fluctuations caused by random sampling, which reduces the steadiness of the final estimate around the average.

Decreasing γ makes each correction smaller. The estimate changes more slowly, but the fluctuations near the average are smaller. This is the speed–accuracy tradeoff represented by γ ↑, speed ↑, accuracy ↓ and by the reversed arrows for a smaller γ.

Optimization seeks methods that improve both speed and accuracy. The tradeoff in these examples explains the problem such methods try to address rather than guaranteeing that every possible algorithm must make exactly the same compromise.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system
teaching: The speech system contains many parts of the tongue, the lips, the velum, the larynx, the palate, and the pharyngeal wall. Their locations and movements jointly determine the changing shape of the vocal tract.

Listing the parts alone does not explain the behavior. Their changing relationships produce the speech movement, just as interacting elements in another biological system produce its behavior.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems
teaching: Voluntary actions and involuntary activities of the heart, pancreas, and neurons can all be studied as dynamical systems. Their elements may be entire organs, parts of organs, individual cells, or chemicals within cells.
Speech is complex because many such elements interact. Biology, chemistry, and physics all study systems whose states change through relationships among their parts.

Two systems can look very different and still share an underlying organization. Studying a simpler system can clarify how a more complicated system changes. Recognizing that deep similarity is an example of moving beyond surface resemblance in creative reasoning.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action
teaching: Jean Alupay, Jennifer Mather, and Khalil Iskarous’s 2023 paper analyzes the octopus arm slap as a complex natural motor action. The researchers studied an Abdopus octopus filmed in tidal pools in Okinawa, Japan, and analyzed 19 slaps directed at fish.

The measured movement combined rotation and translation of the arms. Rotation changes an arm’s orientation, while translation changes its position. The animal combined these simpler kinematic primitives both serially, one after another, and in parallel, at the same time.

Arm movement was measured in an external reference frame and in a reference frame centered on the animal. Combining a small number of movement dimensions allowed controlled behavior while preserving flexibility, a combination the authors call flexible rigidity.

The abstract connects these results with Flash and Hochner’s embodied organization account of motor behavior. Motor primitives can combine in a structured way to produce a complex action. Feed-forward movement primitives work together with sensory feedback about the moving fish, allowing the animal to coordinate its action with its changing environment.

The book reference is Octopus The Ocean’s Intelligent Invertebrate by Jennifer A. Mather, Roland C. Anderson, and James B. Wood. The research article is in Marine Biology 170, article 99, with DOI 10.1007/s00227-023-04243-y.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution
teaching: The input word representations are vectors called x’s or tokens. For the sequence chickens, cackle, and, ducks, each representation contains many numbers rather than a written word that a computer can directly understand.

Weights W carry the model’s learned knowledge. Arithmetic combines the input vectors with those weights and produces a probability distribution over possible next words. The labelled alternatives include a, cat, quack, and Zulu.

The hand-drawn distribution assigns different heights to different candidate words. A higher part of the curve means greater predicted probability, not greater loudness or a later point in time. Its axes have no numerical calibration, so it supports a qualitative comparison rather than exact probabilities.
The transformation from input vectors through weights to a prediction is organized as a dynamical system. The same input can lead to a different distribution when learning changes the weights.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful
teaching: Learning begins with random weights. The model combines them with the input vectors to make a prediction, so its initial output can assign high probability to an inappropriate completion.

For “chickens cackle and ducks,” the known completion is quack. The supplied green prediction peaks at a different candidate, while the red target distribution concentrates probability at quack. The discrepancy tells training that the current weight configuration produces the wrong pattern of output probabilities.
The weights change so that the output distribution better matches the known completion. Repeating prediction and correction over many sequences lets the weights acquire information from the data.

Fake it till you make it names this process of starting without the correct knowledge and improving through feedback. Random guessing alone does not create knowledge. The repeated error-based change of weights is what makes the initial guess useful.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average
teaching: For the three numbers 10, 12, and 14, adding the values and dividing by three gives 12. That direct arithmetic method produces their average when all three values are available.

Complex examples such as speech, language, biological molecules, and scenes do not reduce to adding a few observed numbers. The course therefore uses a different way of learning the average as a model for a more general learning process.

Begin with a guess x, compare it with one observed value from the list, and move the guess part of the way toward that observation. Repeat with another value. Each correction changes the estimate because new evidence exposes a discrepancy. This is observation-based error learning.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters
teaching: The full path begins at 130 and ends near 80 after 12 corrections. Update number is horizontal, estimate x is vertical, the red line tracks the estimate, and the green line marks the data average of 80.25.
The estimate usually falls in this run, but it rises after observations of 98 when the current estimate is below 98. The path therefore jitters rather than descending smoothly to a fixed number.

Stochastic means that observations are randomly selected. Gradient identifies the error-related direction of correction, and descent refers to reducing the mistake. The two central steps are making an initial guess and improving it with data.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls
teaching: The second dataset is [62, 70, 78, 82, 90, 98] and has average 80. The mean-motion rule displayed is x[t+1] = x[t] − 0.25(x[t] − 80). This uses the data average to express the overall tendency of the stochastic process.

Starting at x[0] = 140 puts the estimate above 80. The correction subtracts a quarter of the remaining difference, so the red estimate decreases toward the green target of 80 over the 12 updates on the upper graph.

The displayed loss is L[t] = ½(x[t] − 80)². Squaring the discrepancy makes this measure nonnegative and makes large discrepancies count more strongly. The lower graph plots loss vertically against update number horizontally, beginning at about 1,800 and falling toward zero.
The estimate and the loss both decline in this example because the estimate begins above its target. Their matching directions are a consequence of this initial condition.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls
teaching: The dataset, average of 80, and learning rate of 25% remain the same. The changed initial condition is x[0] = −100, so the estimate begins below the target.
The red estimate now rises toward the green target of 80 on the upper graph. Its difference from the target becomes smaller even though the estimate itself becomes numerically larger.

The lower graph plots ½(x − 80)² against update number. Its loss begins at about 16,200 and decreases toward zero. Squared loss decreases whenever the discrepancy shrinks, whether the estimate approaches from below or from above.

Descent therefore describes the direction of the loss, not a requirement that the estimate fall. The same correction principle can make the estimate move upward or downward depending on which side of the target it occupies.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition
teaching: Each panel plots the estimate x on the vertical axis against epochs from 0 to 300 on the horizontal axis. Red begins at 130, green at 80, and blue at 10. The three initial conditions approach the same general region near the data average of about 80.

At a 10% learning rate, the high red estimate drops and the low blue estimate rises fairly quickly. Once they reach the central region, all three estimates continue to fluctuate modestly because each sampled observation can pull them in a different direction.

At 50%, the initial correction is much faster, but the estimates fluctuate more strongly around the central region. At 80%, the estimates make still larger changes in response to individual observations and remain especially variable.

At 1%, red decreases and blue increases much more slowly. Even by epoch 300, the blue estimate remains below the central region and red approaches it from above. The green estimate stays close to 80 with small fluctuations because it begins near the average and uses small corrections.

A large learning rate gives each observation more influence. That makes the initial response faster but also makes an estimate near the average more vulnerable to being pulled away by a particular data point. A small rate reduces that jitter but requires more observations to travel far from a poor initial guess.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff
teaching: Increasing the learning rate γ increases how quickly an estimate reacts to observations. It also increases the continuing fluctuations caused by random sampling, which reduces the steadiness of the final estimate around the average.

Decreasing γ makes each correction smaller. The estimate changes more slowly, but the fluctuations near the average are smaller. This is the speed–accuracy tradeoff represented by γ ↑, speed ↑, accuracy ↓ and by the reversed arrows for a smaller γ.

Optimization seeks methods that improve both speed and accuracy. The tradeoff in these examples explains the problem such methods try to address rather than guaranteeing that every possible algorithm must make exactly the same compromise.

sections.title: A staged shortest-path problem
teaching: The problem is to reach J from A at the smallest total cost. Circles are states, arrows are allowed transitions, and numbers beside arrows are transition costs. Arrows run through the stages A, then B/C, then D/E/F, then G/H/I, then J.
From A, going to B costs 12 and going to C costs 7. From B, the costs to D, E, and F are 5, 6, and 9. From C, the corresponding costs are 14, 10, and 11.
From D, the costs to G, H, and I are 8, 7, and 10. From E, they are 9, 7, and 9. From F, they are 10, 7, and 8. The final costs are 5 from G to J, 9 from H to J, and 8 from I to J.

A route’s total includes every arrow it follows. Choosing a cheap first transition cannot by itself establish that the full route is cheapest, because later transitions can reverse its apparent advantage.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose
teaching: A greedy algorithm chooses the cheapest available transition at the current state. Here it selects A→C because 7 is smaller than 12, then C→E because 10 is smaller than 14 or 11.
At E it selects H because the immediate cost 7 is smaller than either cost of 9. The final H→J transition costs 9. This route A→C→E→H→J totals 33.
The local choices ignore costs still ahead. An apparently expensive first step can lead to a cheaper complete route, so greed at each immediate edge can give a suboptimal result.

sections.title: Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty
teaching: An exhaustive algorithm considers every complete allowed route from A to J and compares their total costs. Because it evaluates the complete routes, it can identify the true minimum for this finite problem.

Adding states and stages creates many possible combinations of transitions. Enumerating all complete routes can therefore take a very long time even though the selection rule is straightforward. Accuracy is obtained at the cost of inefficient search as the problem grows.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition
teaching: Let V_BJ mean the best remaining cost from B to J, and let V_CJ mean the best remaining cost from C to J. If those values are known, a decision at A can compare two complete possibilities.

The visible equation is V_AJ = min{12 + V_BJ, 7 + V_CJ}. The 12 and 7 pay for the immediate step from A. The successor values pay for the best continuation after that step. Taking the smaller sum identifies the best full route from A.
A value carries the cost of the remaining problem. It differs from the cost printed on a single arrow because it accounts for all the stages still to come.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values
teaching: The best values from B and C are initially unknown, so they become smaller problems to solve. Each asks for the cheapest continuation from one state to the common goal J.

Bellman’s idea is to break a large problem into subproblems whose answers can be used to solve the original problem. Repeating the decomposition eventually reaches states whose remaining costs are directly available.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward
teaching: The final transitions provide the first known values. V_GJ is 5, V_HJ is 9, and V_IJ is 8 because each of these states has a direct arrow to J.

At D, compare 8 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, and 10 + V_IJ. At E, compare 9 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, and 9 + V_IJ. At F, compare 10 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, and 8 + V_IJ. Each comparison combines one immediate cost with a complete remaining value.
With those three values available, B compares 5 + V_DJ, 6 + V_EJ, and 9 + V_FJ. C compares 14 + V_DJ, 10 + V_EJ, and 11 + V_FJ. A then compares its alternatives through B and C.
The direction of computation runs backward from the goal to the start because knowing a later state’s best continuation makes the preceding state’s decision solvable.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values
teaching: Backward evaluation gives D a remaining value of 13 through G, E a value of 14 through G, and F a value of 15 through G. These include the final cost of reaching J.

B therefore has value 18 through D, and C has value 24 through E. At A, the full alternatives are 12 + 18 through B and 7 + 24 through C. The best route begins with the more expensive immediate transition to B because its continuation is sufficiently cheaper.

The shortest route is A→B→D→G→J with total cost 30. Once the remaining values are known, each forward choice can use the minimum of immediate cost plus successor value. That informed local choice retains information about the future.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future
teaching: A costly final transition such as H→J with cost 9 can make an earlier cheap decision unattractive. The difficulty is not visible if the decision maker looks only at the current arrow.

Dynamic programming carries the effect of that future cost backward through the state values. Present choices can then respond to obstacles that lie many stages away because the value of each continuation already includes them.

Kierkegaard’s statement that life is understood backward but lived forward is used as an analogy. The calculation runs backward from a known goal, then the selected route is followed forward from the start.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction
teaching: A large route problem depends on smaller route problems. Each smaller problem can depend on still smaller ones until the remaining route is simple enough to evaluate directly.

Solving those simple terminal problems makes the preceding problems solvable. Their results then support the larger problems. This repeated reuse of solved subproblems reconstructs the answer to the original problem.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value
teaching: For every possible next state, add the cost of reaching that state to its known best remaining value. The smallest of those sums becomes the best value of the current state.
Repeating this rule stage by stage propagates future costs backward. The same comparison works at every state even though the number and costs of available transitions can differ.
The result is both a minimum total cost and a way to choose the route. Store which successor produced the minimum, then follow those choices from the starting state toward the goal.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge
teaching: When movement has the same speed throughout a uniform stretch of sand, the straight shortest path also minimizes travel time. The constant-speed diagrams show a direct route between two people on land.

When a rescuer runs faster on sand than they can swim through water, the fastest route can spend more distance on land before entering the water. The route bends at the shore because an extra distance in the faster region can save time in the slower region.

The shortest-path graph uses the same broad principle. Paying the larger immediate cost of 12 can lead to the cheaper overall route, just as taking a longer physical route in one region can reduce total travel time. The relevant quantity is total cost or total time across the whole route.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle
teaching: Light moves faster through air than through water in the comparison. A light path can change direction at the boundary between the two media, just as a fastest rescue route changes direction at the boundary between faster running and slower swimming.
The pencil in water appears bent because light reaching the observer follows a path that changes direction across the water–air boundary. The physical pencil is not bent by that viewing effect.

The shared idea is that behavior across a whole path depends on the costs of its different portions. A locally shorter or cheaper portion is not always the best choice when the remaining portions occur under different conditions.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values
teaching: The handwritten terminal labels assign G a value of 5 with successor J, H a value of 9 with successor J, and I a value of 8 with successor J.

sections.title: Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium
teaching: The learning graph plots estimate x against epochs from 0 to 300 at a 10% learning rate. Red begins at 130, green at 80, and blue at 10. Red falls and blue rises toward the same central region around 80, with continued jitter from randomly selected observations.

The coffee graph plots temperature in degrees Celsius against time in minutes from 0 to 8. A dashed horizontal line marks room temperature at 18°C. Hot coffee beginning at about 60°C, 80°C, or 100°C cools toward that level, while iced coffee beginning near 0°C, 5°C, or 10°C warms toward it.

The change is large when the difference from the central or equilibrium level is large, and it slows as that difference shrinks. Different initial conditions can therefore approach the same equilibrium from opposite sides.

The shared organization is a correction that opposes a discrepancy. Temperature responds to a difference from the room, while the learning estimate responds to a difference from observations. The coffee curves are smooth, whereas the sampled learning paths remain noisy near their central level.
